title: Cornell Climate Education and Community Engagement Online Course 2026: Global Certificate Program and Scholarships
summary: Applications are open for the Climate Education and Community Engagement online course offered by the Cornell Civic Ecology Lab at Cornell University. The four-week global course is designed for educators, students, community leaders, NGO professionals, volunteers, parents and other individuals interested in connecting climate knowledge with practical education and community action. The course will run online from September 8 to October 4, 2026. Participants who complete the weekly course requirements and final project will receive a Cornell University PDF certificate documenting 25 professional development hours. No previous background in climate science is required, and participants from all countries can register. Tiered tuition is available, with a reduced fee for residents of lower-cost countries and a limited number of competitive need-based scholarships. The deadline to apply for scholarship support is September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time. Climate Education and Community Engagement Course: Key Information Item Details Course title Climate Education and Community Engagement Abbreviation CECE Provider Cornell Civic Ecology Lab Institution Cornell University Course dates September 8–October 4, 2026 Duration Four weeks Format Online and primarily asynchronous Weekly workload Approximately four to five hours Live component Optional live webinar or discussion session Learning platforms edX Edge and Zoom Certificate Cornell University PDF certificate Professional development hours 25 hours Standard fee $90 Reduced fee $20 Scholarship availability Limited, competitive and need-based Scholarship deadline September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. ET Scholarship decisions September 4, 2026 Geographic eligibility Open globally Prior climate-science knowledge Not required About the Climate Education and Community Engagement Course Climate change is frequently discussed as a scientific and environmental issue, but it is also an educational, social, communication and community-development challenge. Educators and community practitioners are increasingly expected to help people understand climate change, identify its local effects, respond constructively to climate anxiety and participate in meaningful action. The Cornell Climate Education and Community Engagement course aims to help learners connect climate knowledge with: Local experience Public communication Education Community participation Youth engagement Climate resilience Adaptation Practical environmental action Rather than treating climate education as the simple transfer of scientific information, the course explores how educators and practitioners can communicate climate issues constructively and help communities identify realistic opportunities for participation and action. The course is delivered by the Cornell Civic Ecology Lab with support from researchers, graduate students and teaching assistants associated with Cornell University’s Department of Natural Resources and the Environment. Full course information is available on the official Climate Education and Community Engagement course page . Course Dates and Duration The 2026 course will run from: September 8 to October 4, 2026 The program lasts four weeks and is delivered online. Participants should plan to spend approximately four to five hours per week completing the course materials, discussions and activities. The certificate documents 25 professional development hours after the learner completes the required weekly work and final project. Because the course is conducted over a defined four-week period, prospective participants should ensure that they can participate regularly throughout the program. Scholarship Application Deadline The deadline to apply for a need-based scholarship is: September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time Scholarship decisions are expected to be announced on: September 4, 2026 The official page does not publish a separate final registration deadline for fee-paying participants. However, because the course begins on September 8, 2026, interested learners should register as early as possible. What Participants Will Learn The course is designed to develop a practical understanding of climate education and community engagement. Participants will explore how to: Build an accurate foundation in climate literacy Explain climate change clearly to different audiences Connect scientific knowledge with local experience Recognize climate risks affecting local communities Identify community strengths, assets and potential partners Communicate climate issues in constructive and action-oriented ways Address climate anxiety through meaningful learning and participation Understand connections between climate change, equity and public participation Explore climate adaptation and community resilience Support youth agency in climate-related learning Move learners from climate awareness toward practical engagement Design a locally relevant climate-education or community-engagement plan The course is intended to help participants translate knowledge into educational or community practice rather than simply complete theoretical lessons. Climate Literacy Climate literacy involves understanding the essential principles of the climate system and the ways climate change affects individuals, communities, ecosystems and institutions. Within an educational or community setting, climate literacy also involves the ability to: Interpret climate information Distinguish reliable evidence from misinformation Explain climate change in accessible language Relate global climate patterns to local experiences Understand risk, adaptation and resilience Communicate uncertainty responsibly Identify meaningful responses Participants will develop a foundation they can use when teaching students, engaging families or working with community groups. Climate Communication Climate information can be technically complex, politically sensitive or emotionally difficult. People may also experience fear, helplessness or anxiety when discussing climate impacts. The course examines how educators and community practitioners can communicate climate change in ways that are: Clear Accurate Understandable Constructive Appropriate for the intended audience Connected with local experience Focused on meaningful action Participants will practice explaining climate issues to a selected audience, which could include: School students University learners Parents Families Community members NGO participants Volunteers Public stakeholders Local decision-makers This audience-focused approach helps learners avoid overly general communication and develop messages suited to their professional or community context. Mapping Local Climate Risks and Community Assets One important component of the course is the identification of local climate risks, community assets and potential partners. Climate risks may include: Extreme heat Flooding Drought Water scarcity Wildfires Air pollution Coastal impacts Agricultural disruption Food insecurity Health risks Infrastructure vulnerability Displacement or livelihood challenges Community assets may include: Schools and universities Local government institutions Community groups Youth organizations NGOs and nonprofit organizations Faith-based groups Health services Local experts Environmental networks Volunteer groups Public spaces Existing climate or sustainability initiatives By considering both risk and community capacity, participants can design activities that respond to actual local needs while building on existing strengths. Community Engagement and Public Participation The course explores climate action as a collaborative process rather than an activity led only by technical experts. Participants consider how communities can become involved in: Identifying local concerns Sharing lived experiences Discussing climate risks Contributing local knowledge Designing educational programs Participating in adaptation planning Developing resilience strategies Supporting youth participation Building partnerships Taking collective action This approach recognizes that communities are not simply recipients of climate information. They can also be active contributors to learning, planning and decision-making. Climate Equity, Adaptation and Resilience Climate change does not affect every population equally. Communities can differ in their exposure to hazards, access to financial resources, infrastructure, political influence and capacity to recover. The course connects climate education with questions of: Equity Inclusion Public participation Local vulnerability Adaptation Community capacity Resilience Environmental justice Participants are encouraged to think about how education and engagement initiatives can respond to diverse community circumstances. Youth Climate Learning and Agency Young people are an important audience for climate education. However, teaching climate change only as a global crisis can produce fear or helplessness. The course explores constructive approaches that help young people: Understand climate change Relate climate issues to their communities Express their concerns Participate in discussions Identify realistic forms of action Build problem-solving skills Develop confidence and agency Work collaboratively with others Parents, teachers, caregivers and community educators can use these approaches to support informed and meaningful youth participation. Course Activities Participants will apply course concepts to a school, organization, community, professional program or project idea of their own. During the course, learners will: Study research-informed learning materials. Watch short instructional videos. Review climate-education and community-engagement case studies. Participate in peer discussions. Identify a climate issue relevant to their local or professional setting. Select a specific audience for climate communication. Practice explaining climate change to that audience. Map local climate risks and community assets. Identify organizations or individuals who could serve as partners. Explore strategies for moving from awareness to participation. Draft a climate-education or community-engagement plan. Refine the plan using course concepts and peer feedback. Submit a final project describing the plan and practical next steps. Final Project The final project is intended to help participants convert their learning into something useful for their own setting. Depending on the participant’s role and context, the project may take the form of: A climate-education lesson plan A nature-education lesson A community program activity A youth-engagement initiative A public climate-communication activity A local awareness campaign A climate-resilience learning activity A community-engagement plan An NGO or nonprofit program concept An adaptation-focused educational activity The final project should outline the learner’s proposed activity, intended audience and practical next steps. Participants must complete the final project, together with the required weekly work, to qualify for the course certificate. Online Course Format The course is primarily asynchronous. This means participants can generally complete weekly materials at times that suit their schedules rather than attending every class at a fixed time. Weekly modules may include: Videos Readings Research-informed materials Case studies Discussion prompts Peer exchanges Reflective exercises Practical activities Project-development tasks The asynchronous structure makes the course accessible across different countries and time zones. Optional Live Component An optional live webinar or discussion session will be included. Participants who cannot attend the live session can access a recording. This is particularly helpful for international participants whose local time zones may make live attendance difficult. The live session may provide an opportunity to: Discuss course themes Hear from instructors or facilitators Ask questions Exchange experiences Learn from other participants Obtain guidance on practical application The official page describes the live component as optional, so participants should not assume that inability to attend live will automatically prevent course completion. Learning Platforms and Technology The course uses: edX Edge for course modules and discussions Zoom for live sessions Prospective learners should have: Reliable internet access A computer, tablet or compatible device A working email address The ability to access edX Edge Access to Zoom if they plan to attend live Basic ability to download, complete and upload files Sufficient English proficiency to understand the course materials and participate in discussions The official course page does not state that advanced technical skills are required. Social and Applied Learning The course uses a learning approach based on: Social learning Reflection Practical application Peer exchange Local relevance Case-study analysis Participants learn by applying course ideas to their own context and sharing examples, resources and feedback with other learners. The global structure allows participants to compare climate-education and engagement experiences from different communities and countries. Who Should Take the Course? The course is designed for a broad global audience. School, informal and community educators Teachers and educators can use the course to strengthen their ability to explain climate change and incorporate constructive climate learning into lessons or programs. NGO and nonprofit professionals Professionals designing climate, sustainability, youth or community initiatives can use the course to improve their engagement strategies and program planning. Community leaders and volunteers Individuals working on local climate action, adaptation, public participation or resilience can learn how to connect community knowledge with educational activities. University students Students interested in environmental studies, education, climate change, public policy, development, communication or community engagement can build a practical foundation through the course. Early-career professionals The course can help early-career professionals understand how climate education and community participation can be incorporated into professional projects. Parents and caregivers Parents, caregivers and family educators can explore practical ways to support climate learning and agency among children and young people. Environmental education professionals Experienced professionals can use the program to update existing environmental-education activities with a stronger focus on climate literacy, communication and action. Eligibility Requirements The course is open globally. The official page does not require: A university degree Previous professional experience Previous climate-science training Employment with an environmental organization Citizenship in a particular country Formal teaching qualifications No prior background in climate science is required. Participants should, however, be prepared to complete approximately four to five hours of weekly coursework and submit a final project. Tuition and Tiered Pricing The Cornell Civic Ecology Lab uses tiered pricing to make the course more accessible to educators and practitioners worldwide. Standard fee: $90 The standard fee applies to residents of: United States Canada European countries Japan South Korea Singapore Mainland China Taiwan Israel Australia New Zealand Reduced fee: $20 The reduced fee applies to participants residing in all other countries. This means residents of many countries in Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, the Middle East and the Pacific can qualify for the reduced rate. The fee category is based on the participant’s country of residence rather than citizenship. Fee for Participants Residing in Pakistan Participants residing in Pakistan fall within the “all other countries” category and should therefore qualify for the reduced $20 fee. Pakistani applicants may also seek one of the limited need-based scholarships if they require financial support. Need-Based Scholarships A limited number of competitive, need-based scholarships are available. The official page does not specify: The number of scholarships The exact monetary value Whether every scholarship covers the complete course fee The number of applicants expected A guaranteed award for any particular country or profession Applicants should therefore understand that financial assistance is limited and competitive. How to Apply for a Scholarship Applicants seeking scholarship support should: Visit the official course page. Download the 2026 CECE Scholarship Application Word document. Complete all required sections of the document. Save the completed document as a PDF. Open the online course-registration form. Upload the PDF as part of the registration process. Submit the registration and scholarship request by September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. ET. Wait for the scholarship decision expected on September 4, 2026. Applicants should complete the scholarship document before beginning the online registration form. Cornell University Certificate Participants who complete the course requirements will receive a Cornell University PDF certificate in Climate Education and Community Engagement. The certificate documents: 25 professional development hours To receive the certificate, participants must complete: Required weekly coursework Relevant activities and discussions The final project The certificate is a professional-development credential. The official page does not state that it carries Cornell academic credit, constitutes admission to Cornell University or can be counted toward a Cornell degree. Participants should not describe themselves as Cornell students or alumni solely on the basis of completing this short online course. Course Team The course is offered by the Cornell Civic Ecology Lab with support from researchers, graduate students and teaching assistants. Fish Yu Fish Yu is associated with Cornell University’s Department of Natural Resources and the Environment. Yu holds a Master of Science from Cornell University with specialization in public participation and climate governance and has worked with environmental educators and sustainability practitioners internationally. Professor Marianne Krasny Professor Marianne Krasny is a scholar in environmental education and civic ecology at Cornell University. She has authored multiple books and research publications, including work informing the course. Alex Kudryavtsev Alex Kudryavtsev is a researcher in sustainability education and urban environmental education at Cornell University. His published work includes a framework for nature education. Hamid Nikzad Hamid Nikzad is a Cornell graduate student conducting research related to agriculture, human well-being and climate change. He serves as the course administrator and supports participant questions. How to Register Interested participants can follow these steps: Read the complete course information. Confirm availability from September 8 to October 4, 2026. Determine whether the standard or reduced fee applies to their country of residence. Decide whether to request need-based scholarship support. Download and complete the scholarship document if applying for assistance. Save the scholarship application as a PDF. Open the official registration form. Provide the requested personal and professional information. Upload the scholarship PDF where applicable. Submit the form. Follow any payment or enrolment instructions received from the course team. Retain a copy of the registration confirmation. Register for the Climate Education and Community Engagement course Important Dates Activity Date Scholarship application deadline September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. ET Scholarship decisions announced September 4, 2026 Course begins September 8, 2026 Course ends October 4, 2026 A separate general registration deadline is not stated on the official course page. Early registration is recommended. Important Points Before Registering Prospective participants should remember that: The course is online. It runs for four weeks. Most learning activities are asynchronous. The optional live session will be recorded. edX Edge is used for modules and discussions. Zoom is used for live activities. The anticipated workload is four to five hours per week. No prior climate-science background is required. Participation is open globally. The standard fee is $90. The reduced fee is $20. Scholarships are limited and competitive. The scholarship deadline is September 1, 2026. Certificate eligibility requires completion of weekly work and the final project. The certificate documents 25 professional development hours. The course is not advertised as an academic-credit program. Contact Information Questions can be directed to: Email: CivicEcology@cornell.edu Applicants should include “CECE” in the email subject line so that the course administrator can identify the inquiry. Conclusion The Cornell Climate Education and Community Engagement online course provides an accessible opportunity for learners worldwide to develop practical skills in climate literacy, communication, local risk assessment, community participation, youth agency and climate resilience. Running from September 8 to October 4, 2026, the course combines asynchronous weekly modules, research-informed materials, short videos, case studies, discussions, practical activities and an optional recorded live session. Participants will apply their learning to a real school, organization, community or project idea and produce a practical climate-education or engagement plan. Those who complete the weekly requirements and final project will receive a Cornell University PDF certificate documenting 25 professional development hours. No previous climate-science training or university degree is required. Tiered pricing makes the course more accessible internationally, while a limited number of competitive, need-based scholarships are available to applicants who submit the required document by September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time. title: Citadel Conference Travel Grant 2026: Fully Funded Conference Travel Support for STEM Students
summary: The Citadel Conference Travel Grant is an opportunity designed to support promising students in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) who want to attend leading academic and research conferences around the world. The program is intended to help rising talent participate in conferences where they can present their research, exchange ideas, connect with researchers and industry professionals, and gain exposure to developments at the forefront of their fields. For selected applicants, Citadel provides substantial financial support covering major conference-related expenses, including the conference registration or full-access pass, round-trip airfare, accommodation, airport transportation, and a food stipend. Recipients may also have opportunities to attend Citadel-hosted dinners and recruitment events during their chosen conference. The grant is particularly relevant to students pursuing mathematics, computer science, physics, statistics, electrical engineering, and other quantitative disciplines . What Is the Citadel Conference Travel Grant? The Citadel Conference Travel Grant is a conference funding initiative created to expand opportunities for exceptional students and emerging STEM researchers. Academic and research conferences are important platforms for students and researchers to: Present research findings Publish and discuss academic work Exchange ideas with experts Discover new developments in their disciplines Build professional networks Meet potential collaborators Learn about career opportunities Gain exposure to leading organizations and researchers However, conference attendance can be expensive, particularly for students who need to travel internationally. The Citadel Conference Travel Grant aims to reduce this financial barrier by providing selected students with comprehensive travel support. What Does the Citadel Conference Travel Grant Cover? Selected applicants can receive support for several major expenses associated with attending an eligible conference. 1. Full-Access Conference Pass Citadel will cover the entire cost of a full-access conference pass for selected applicants. This allows recipients to participate in the eligible conference without having to personally cover the conference registration cost. Important: The full-access conference pass benefit does not apply to the Grace Hopper Celebration. 2. Round-Trip Airfare Citadel will provide round-trip airfare for selected recipients. This is particularly valuable for students attending international conferences because airfare can represent a significant portion of the total cost of conference participation. 3. Accommodation Selected students will receive lodging support for the duration of their conference participation. The accommodation is arranged through Citadel s designated travel arrangements. 4. Airport and Local Transportation Recipients will receive travel support for transportation to and from the airport. Citadel also provides Uber vouchers for transportation during the conference week. 5. Food Stipend Grant recipients will receive a meal stipend to help cover food expenses during their conference attendance. Details regarding the food stipend are provided to selected recipients at a later stage. 6. Exclusive Citadel Events Selected recipients may have the opportunity to participate in Citadel-hosted dinners and recruitment events associated with their chosen conference. These events can provide students with opportunities to meet Citadel professionals and learn more about careers and work in quantitative and technology-focused fields. Who Is the Citadel Conference Travel Grant For? The program is designed for students who are currently pursuing: Bachelor s degrees Master s degrees PhD programs Citadel is particularly interested in applicants studying: Mathematics Computer Science Physics Statistics Electrical Engineering Other quantitative disciplines Students in related quantitative fields may also be considered. Preference for Research Conference Applicants For applicants attending research conferences where papers are published, preference may be given to students who have submitted at least one paper to the conference. Examples of research-focused conferences include major events such as: ICML NeurIPS ICLR ACL Submitting a paper does not necessarily mean that every applicant will be selected, but research involvement can strengthen an application where applicable. What Does Citadel Look For in Applicants? Selection is based on several factors. Academic Performance The selection panel considers the applicant s academic performance and overall record. Students with strong academic achievements may be more competitive. Research and Publication Record Applicants with research experience and publications may receive favorable consideration. For conferences that publish academic papers, submitting or presenting research can strengthen an application. Awards and Previous Achievements The panel also considers previous awards and other evidence of academic or professional accomplishment. Applicants should therefore highlight relevant: Academic awards Research awards Competitions Scholarships Publications Research projects Other notable achievements Presentation and Conference Involvement Citadel gives priority to applicants who are actively involved in their chosen conference. This may include: Presenting a research paper Presenting a poster Participating actively in the conference Applicants who are presenting or otherwise contributing to the academic program can demonstrate a stronger connection between the conference and their research or professional development. This preference does not apply to the Grace Hopper Celebration. Potential Impact The selection panel also considers the potential impact that attending the conference could have on: The applicant s research Academic development Professional development Future career Citadel s objectives Applicants should therefore be able to explain why attending the particular conference is important to their academic or professional goals. Eligible Conferences The current conference travel grant program identifies several eligible conferences. These include: Grace Hopper Celebration NeurIPS – Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems Joint March Meeting and April Meeting – Global Physics Summit ICLR – International Conference on Learning Representations ICML – International Conference on Machine Learning ACL – Association for Computational Linguistics Applicants should check the specific conference requirements and application deadlines because timelines vary from one conference to another. Upcoming Conference Opportunities NeurIPS 2026 Conference: NeurIPS – Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems Location: Sydney, Australia Conference Dates: December 6–12, 2026 Application Deadline: October 5, 2026 Applicant Notification: October 9, 2026 NeurIPS is a major international conference focused on machine learning, artificial intelligence, and related areas. Students whose research aligns with machine learning, AI, statistics, computer science, and related quantitative disciplines may find this conference particularly relevant. Grace Hopper Celebration 2026 Location: Anaheim, California, USA Conference Dates: October 27–30, 2026 Application Deadline: September 25, 2026 Applicant Notification: October 5, 2026 The Grace Hopper Celebration is one of the major conferences associated with women in computing and technology. Applicants interested in attending this conference should note that it has specific grant arrangements and requirements. Most importantly, the standard full-access conference pass coverage described for other eligible conferences does not apply to the Grace Hopper Celebration. Applicants should therefore carefully review the conference-specific terms before applying. Important Deadlines at a Glance Because the Citadel Conference Travel Grant supports multiple conferences, there is not one universal application deadline . Applicants must follow the deadline associated with the specific conference they wish to attend. NeurIPS 2026 Application Deadline: October 5, 2026 Notification: October 9, 2026 Grace Hopper Celebration 2026 Application Deadline: September 25, 2026 Notification: October 5, 2026 Applicants interested in other eligible conferences should consult the Citadel Conference Travel Grant page for the applicable conference-specific timeline. How the Grant Is Delivered Selected applicants do not simply receive a lump-sum travel payment. Citadel manages many of the travel arrangements directly. The process generally includes: Citadel purchasing the conference pass directly Flights being arranged through Citadel s travel agency Hotel accommodation being booked through the travel agency Uber vouchers being provided for airport and local transportation Food stipend information being provided to recipients This approach helps selected students focus on participating in the conference rather than managing the major travel expenses themselves. Must Applicants Attend in Person? Yes. Selected applicants are expected to attend the conference in person . Students who are only presenting remotely or participating virtually are not eligible for the travel grant on that basis. The purpose of the grant is to facilitate physical participation at eligible conferences and enable recipients to benefit from direct networking, presentations, discussions, and professional engagement. Can Students Apply for Multiple Conferences? Yes. Students may apply for the Citadel Conference Travel Grant for multiple conferences within the same year. There is no stated limit on the number of conference travel grants an applicant can apply for . However, applicants should ensure that they meet the eligibility and conference-specific requirements for every application they submit. Are There Post-Conference Requirements? No. Selected recipients do not have to provide a report or presentation after attending the conference. There are no post-conference obligations specified for successful grant recipients. Read Full Details HERE How to Strengthen Your Application Students interested in this opportunity should prepare a strong application that clearly demonstrates their academic and professional potential. Consider highlighting: Academic Excellence Include relevant academic achievements and demonstrate your strength in your field of study. Research Experience Explain your current research interests, projects, publications, or other research activities. Conference Participation If applicable, clearly state whether you will: Present a paper Present a poster Participate in a research session Contribute to the conference in another meaningful way Publications If you have published academic research, make sure relevant publications are clearly presented. Awards Include significant academic, research, technology, or professional awards. Conference Relevance Explain why attending the specific conference is important to your work and how participation could contribute to your academic or professional development. A𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐲 HERE Why the Citadel Conference Travel Grant Matters For students, attending an international research conference can be a transformative academic and professional experience. A conference can provide opportunities to: Learn from leading researchers Discover emerging developments Receive feedback on research Meet potential collaborators Build an international professional network Explore career opportunities Gain confidence presenting research Understand current challenges within a discipline The cost of international conference participation, however, can prevent many talented students from attending. By covering major travel and participation expenses, the Citadel Conference Travel Grant helps reduce this barrier and gives selected students the opportunity to participate in leading conferences. Conclusion The Citadel Conference Travel Grant offers an excellent opportunity for ambitious STEM students to participate in leading academic and research conferences without having to personally shoulder the major costs of international conference travel. Through support for conference passes, flights, accommodation, transportation, and meals, the program enables students to focus on research, learning, networking, and professional development. The opportunity is particularly valuable for students in mathematics, computer science, physics, statistics, electrical engineering, and other quantitative disciplines , especially those with strong academic records, research experience, publications, awards, or active involvement in conferences. Students should carefully review the conference-specific requirements and deadlines. For the currently listed 2026 opportunities, the Grace Hopper Celebration deadline is September 25, 2026 , while the NeurIPS deadline is October 5, 2026 . For complete information and to apply, applicants should visit the official Citadel Conference Travel Grant page and review the requirements for their chosen conference. title: Central Asia Youth Dialogue Forum 2026 in Kyrgyzstan: Fully Funded OSCE Workshop on Preventing Youth Engagement in Criminal Activities
summary: Young people across Central Asia are increasingly playing an important role in strengthening communities, promoting social development and addressing emerging security challenges. However, youth can also face vulnerabilities that may expose them to organized crime, drug trafficking, online criminal activities, financial crime and other forms of exploitation. To address these challenges, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) is inviting young people from Central Asia to participate in the Central Asia Youth Dialogue Forum 2026: “Preventing Youth Engagement in Criminal Activities.” This regional workshop will take place from 5 to 9 October 2026 in Issyk-Kul, Kyrgyzstan , bringing together up to 25 young participants for five days of dialogue, interactive learning, networking and youth-led project development. The forum is designed for young people who are interested in building safer and more resilient communities and who want to contribute to preventing youth involvement in criminal activities across the Central Asian region. Central Asia Youth Dialogue Forum 2026 Overview The Central Asia Youth Dialogue Forum is a regional youth-focused initiative organized by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) through the Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities. The programme will provide selected participants with an opportunity to examine some of the major crime and security challenges affecting young people and communities across Central Asia. Participants will not only learn about existing crime-prevention approaches but will also work collaboratively to develop practical, youth-led solutions. An important component of the programme will involve developing project ideas and pitching them to international organizations and donors that support youth-led initiatives. The forum will therefore combine knowledge development, regional dialogue, practical project development, networking and community engagement . Event Details Opportunity: Central Asia Youth Dialogue Forum 2026 Theme: Preventing Youth Engagement in Criminal Activities Organized by: Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) Organizing office: Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities Opportunity field: Youth Dates: 5–9 October 2026 Location: Issyk-Kul, Kyrgyzstan Number of participants: Up to 25 young people Participation: In person Participation fee: No registration or participation fee Travel support: Covered for selected participants Accommodation: Covered for selected participants Meals: Covered for selected participants Training materials: Covered for selected participants Application deadline: 26 August 2026 at 17:00 CEST What Is the Central Asia Youth Dialogue Forum About? The forum focuses on the prevention of youth engagement in criminal activities and seeks to strengthen young people s understanding of emerging security and social challenges in Central Asia. Young people can be particularly vulnerable to criminal recruitment and exploitation. Factors such as unemployment, social exclusion, lack of educational opportunities, online manipulation and economic vulnerability can create conditions that criminal groups may exploit. The OSCE forum will create a space where young people from Central Asian countries can examine these challenges from a regional perspective and identify approaches that can help communities become more resilient. Rather than simply providing theoretical training, the programme will encourage participants to think about practical solutions that young people can implement in their own communities. Key Topics Covered During the Forum Participants will take part in interactive learning sessions covering several areas related to crime prevention and youth engagement. 1. Organized Crime Recruitment Participants will explore how organized criminal groups recruit and exploit young people and examine the factors that can make youth vulnerable to criminal involvement. Understanding recruitment patterns can help young leaders, educators, community organizations and policymakers develop more effective prevention strategies. 2. Drug Trafficking Drug trafficking is an important regional security concern, and young people can be affected both as potential victims of criminal exploitation and as members of communities experiencing the consequences of drug-related crime. The forum will provide participants with an opportunity to better understand the challenges associated with drug trafficking and consider approaches to prevention. 3. Financial Crime and Money Laundering The programme will also address financial crime and money laundering. Participants can expect to explore how illicit financial activities operate and why financial integrity and awareness are important components of preventing and combating criminal activities. This knowledge can be particularly valuable for young people interested in governance, economics, law, finance, development and public policy. 4. Online Risks and Social Media Digital platforms have created new opportunities for communication and education, but they have also introduced new risks. The forum will examine online risks and the role of social media in relation to youth vulnerability and criminal activities. Participants will have an opportunity to consider how digital literacy, responsible online engagement and community awareness can contribute to preventing young people from becoming victims or participants in criminal activities. 5. Gender Dimensions of Crime Prevention The forum will also examine the gender dimensions associated with crime and prevention. Understanding how criminal activities and vulnerabilities can affect different groups differently is important for developing inclusive and effective prevention initiatives. 6. Evidence-Based Prevention Approaches Participants will learn about approaches to preventing youth engagement in criminal activities that are informed by evidence and practical experience. This can help young leaders move beyond general awareness campaigns and develop initiatives based on identified needs, evidence and measurable outcomes. 7. Project Development and Pitching A practical component of the programme will focus on project development. Participants will work with their peers to develop youth-led initiatives designed to strengthen community resilience against crime. They will also have an opportunity to pitch their project ideas to international organizations and donors supporting youth-led solutions. This element can help participants develop important skills in: Identifying community problems Developing project concepts Designing youth-led interventions Working collaboratively Presenting ideas Communicating project impact Engaging potential partners Pitching projects to donors and international organizations Why Participate in the Central Asia Youth Dialogue Forum? The OSCE forum offers participants several opportunities for personal, professional and community development. Build Knowledge and Expertise Participants will gain exposure to a range of issues connected to youth crime prevention, organized crime, drug trafficking, financial crime, online risks and community resilience. The interactive nature of the sessions is designed to help participants engage with these topics rather than simply receive information through lectures. Develop Youth-Led Solutions One of the most practical benefits of the programme is the opportunity to work with other young people to develop innovative initiatives. Participants can use their understanding of local and regional challenges to develop projects that seek to prevent youth involvement in criminal activities and strengthen community resilience. Pitch Ideas to International Organizations and Donors Participants will have the opportunity to present their project ideas to international organizations and donors supporting youth-led solutions. This can provide valuable exposure to how development and community projects are communicated to potential supporters. It can also help participants strengthen their project-pitching and advocacy skills. Expand Your Regional Network The forum will bring together young people from across Central Asia, creating an opportunity to establish connections with peers who share an interest in youth development, community engagement, security and crime prevention. Participants can potentially build relationships with: Young leaders Youth activists Community representatives Practitioners Experts International organizations Other stakeholders working on crime prevention and youth development Regional networks can be valuable for future collaborations, youth initiatives and community projects. Participate Without Paying a Registration Fee Selected participants will not be required to pay a registration or participation fee. This makes the programme accessible to eligible young people who may otherwise face financial barriers to participating in an international regional event. What Costs Does the OSCE Cover? For selected participants, the OSCE will provide comprehensive participation support. The programme covers: Travel Accommodation Meals Training materials Participants therefore do not need to pay a registration or participation fee to attend the forum. Applicants should nevertheless carefully review the official application information for any additional logistical instructions concerning travel and participation. Who Can Apply for the Central Asia Youth Dialogue Forum? The opportunity is specifically intended for young people from the five Central Asian countries represented in the programme. Applicants must meet all of the core eligibility requirements established by the organizers. Age Requirement Applicants must be 18 to 25 years old by 4 October 2026 . This means applicants must fall within the specified age range immediately before the forum begins. Citizenship Requirement Applicants must be citizens of one of the following countries: Kazakhstan Kyrgyzstan Tajikistan Turkmenistan Uzbekistan The programme is therefore specifically targeted at young people from Central Asia rather than applicants from other regions of the world. title: OECD Research Internship in Employment, Labour and Social Affairs Apply by 4 September 2026
summary: The OECD Directorate for Employment, Labour and Social Affairs (ELS) is offering a research-oriented internship for a highly qualified and motivated student with a background in economics or applied social sciences . The internship is based within the Jobs and Income Division of ELS , the team responsible for important OECD research on labour markets, employment, job quality and working conditions. The role provides an opportunity to work alongside economists on research examining labour shortages and workers’ preferences , while gaining experience in an international policy and research environment. The internship is particularly suited to students with strong quantitative research, econometric, analytical and writing skills who are interested in applied labour economics and evidence-based policymaking. Internship Overview The intern will contribute to a new research project examining why labour shortages persist in certain occupations and sectors and how workers value different characteristics of jobs. The project uses an original survey incorporating a discrete choice experiment to investigate workers preferences regarding different job characteristics. Depending on the priorities of the team and the candidate s skills, the intern may also contribute to related OECD research covering: Working time across countries. Job quality. Labour market transitions. Labour shortages. Workers preferences. Comparative labour market research. The internship also provides exposure to the OECD s wider policy and research environment, including seminars, discussions with experts and opportunities to present work in an international setting. Who Can Apply? The opportunity is open to students who meet the following requirements: Must be a national of an OECD member country . Must be enrolled in a full-time graduate degree programme in economics or a closely related field throughout the entire internship. The position is particularly suited to students at an advanced stage of their studies, including: PhD candidates. Master s students in the final year of their programme. Must be available for at least four months . Must have an excellent command of English . Must have strong writing, drafting and communication skills. Must possess solid quantitative research abilities. Must have familiarity with statistical or econometric software such as Stata, R or Python . Must be comfortable working in a multicultural and international environment. APPLY HERE Additional Skills That Would Be an Advantage Some skills are not mandatory but would strengthen an application. These include: Knowledge of German , particularly because the research survey will be conducted in Germany. Experience with survey design. Experience with questionnaire testing. Knowledge of discrete choice experiments. Experience estimating discrete choice models. Previous empirical research experience. Experience working with large or complex datasets. Knowledge of German is specifically described as a strong advantage but is not mandatory . What Will the Intern Work On? The successful candidate will work closely with economists in the ELS Directorate. Responsibilities may include several stages of the research process. 1. Developing the Survey The intern may contribute to developing a survey instrument that incorporates a discrete choice experiment. This can involve: Selecting relevant attributes. Designing the experimental component. Developing the questionnaire. Drafting survey questions. Ensuring that the survey can effectively capture workers preferences. 2. Testing the Survey Before the survey is fully launched, the intern may participate in testing its design. This can involve: Conducting cognitive interviews. Supporting a soft launch. Reviewing feedback. Identifying problems with the questionnaire. Revising the instrument based on testing results. This provides practical experience with the process of turning a research concept into a functioning empirical survey. 3. Working With the Survey Company The intern may also liaise with a professional survey company responsible for elements of the research process. Tasks can include supporting work related to: Survey scripting. Translation. Sampling. Quality control. Fieldwork monitoring. This gives the intern exposure to the operational side of large-scale empirical research. 4. Analysing the Data Once the survey data have been collected, the intern may contribute to quantitative analysis. Responsibilities may include: Analysing survey data. Constructing tables. Producing figures. Conducting robustness checks. Supporting empirical research and interpretation. Strong quantitative skills are therefore particularly important for this position. Technical and Research Skills This internship is strongly research-oriented, meaning applicants should be comfortable working with quantitative evidence. Experience with statistical and econometric tools such as: Stata R Python is expected. Applicants should also be able to demonstrate their ability to communicate empirical findings clearly through written research. Previous experience with survey design, discrete choice experiments or empirical labour-market research can further strengthen an application. Shortlisted Candidates Applicants who are shortlisted may be asked to participate in an additional technical discussion. The discussion may focus on: A submitted writing sample. Previous empirical research. Data construction. Methodological decisions. Limitations of the analysis. The applicant s approach to empirical research. Shortlisted candidates may also be asked to provide a reference letter from an academic supervisor or previous employer. Applicants should therefore be prepared to discuss their research work in detail and explain not only what they did, but also why they selected particular methods and what limitations their analysis has. Internship Duration The internship has a minimum duration of four months . It can be extended for up to six months . The preferred arrangement is a full-time internship of approximately 40 hours per week . Start Date The expected start date is: Mid- to late October 2026, or as soon as possible thereafter. Location and Working Arrangement The internship is based at OECD headquarters in Paris, France . The preferred arrangement is in-person , although partial remote work may be possible. This provides interns with the opportunity to work directly within an international organisation and interact with economists, researchers and policy professionals from different countries. Internship Allowance The OECD provides a monthly allowance of: EUR 1,000 per month This financial support is intended to contribute toward the intern s living expenses during the internship. Applicants should nevertheless consider the cost of living in Paris when planning for the internship period. Writing Sample Applicants must provide a recent piece of empirical work written in English . The writing sample should preferably be sole-authored rather than co-authored , allowing the selection team to assess the applicant s individual research and writing abilities. A strong writing sample should demonstrate: Clear research questions. Appropriate methodology. Quantitative analysis. Good data interpretation. Strong academic writing. Awareness of methodological limitations. 3. Cover Letter Applicants should also submit a short and concise cover letter . The cover letter should explain why the candidate is interested in the internship and why their academic and research background makes them suitable for the position. Applications should be sent to: andrea.garnero@oecd.org How to Make Your Application Competitive Because this is a research-focused position, applicants should make sure their application demonstrates more than simply an interest in economics. Conclusion The OECD Directorate for Employment, Labour and Social Affairs Internship is a strong opportunity for advanced Master s and PhD students interested in economics, labour markets, applied social science and quantitative research . title: AfCFTA and ADAPT: Building a Connected Digital Single Market for Africa
summary: The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is one of Africa’s most ambitious efforts to create a more integrated and connected continental economy. The agreement is designed to reduce barriers to trade, encourage the movement of goods and services across African borders, and create greater opportunities for businesses, entrepreneurs and consumers. A major part of achieving this vision is digitalisation. As African economies become increasingly dependent on digital platforms, electronic payments, digital identity and data-driven services, Africa needs the digital infrastructure that allows businesses and people to participate in cross-border trade more easily. This is where Africa Digital Access and Public Infrastructure for Trade (ADAPT) comes in. What Is the African Continental Free Trade Area? The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is a flagship project of the African Union s Agenda 2063: The Africa We Want . Its central ambition is to create a more integrated African market by reducing barriers that make it difficult and expensive to trade across national borders. The agreement covers a broad range of economic activities, including: Trade in goods Trade in services Digital trade Investment Trade facilitation Economic integration Cross-border business activity Rather than African countries operating primarily as separate national markets, AfCFTA seeks to make it easier for businesses to reach customers and partners across the continent. The long-term objective is to increase intra-African trade , particularly trade involving value-added goods and services produced within Africa. Why Creating One African Market Matters Africa has a large and diverse consumer and business market, but trade between African countries can still be complicated by differences in regulations, customs procedures, payment systems, identification systems, logistics and access to information. These barriers can make cross-border business more expensive and time-consuming, particularly for smaller businesses. AfCFTA aims to address these challenges by creating a framework for greater economic integration. The figures provided by the AfCFTA Secretariat illustrate the scale of the project: 54 AU member states had signed the AfCFTA Agreement as of January 2025. 50 State Parties were reported as of February 2026. The initiative has the potential to help lift 30 million people out of extreme poverty . Estimates indicate a potential $450 billion increase in income in Africa by 2035 , representing approximately a 7% gain. These figures demonstrate why AfCFTA is much more than a conventional trade agreement. It represents an attempt to reshape how African economies interact with one another. APPLY HERE What Is ADAPT? Africa Digital Access and Public Infrastructure for Trade (ADAPT) is designed to provide the digital infrastructure needed to help make the AfCFTA vision practical. The basic idea is straightforward: you cannot build an effective single African market without the digital systems that allow people and businesses to interact across borders. ADAPT focuses on connecting critical digital components, particularly: Digital identity Data infrastructure Digital payments Access to digital services Infrastructure supporting cross-border trade By bringing these systems together, ADAPT can help reduce some of the practical barriers that businesses face when attempting to operate across African markets. The Role of Digital Identity Digital identity can play an important role in cross-border commerce. Businesses and individuals frequently need to prove who they are when accessing financial services, registering businesses, completing transactions or interacting with government systems. Interoperable digital identity infrastructure can potentially make these processes more efficient by allowing trusted digital credentials to be used across different systems. For businesses operating across borders, this could mean: Easier verification More efficient onboarding Reduced administrative processes Greater access to digital financial services Improved trust between businesses and customers The Importance of Data Data is another fundamental component of a modern digital economy. Businesses need reliable information about markets, customers, regulations, prices and trade opportunities. Governments also need data to understand economic activity and design effective policies. ADAPT s focus on digital infrastructure can therefore support a more connected data environment for African trade. Better digital data systems can help create opportunities for: Market intelligence Digital commerce Trade information Business registration Regulatory compliance Economic planning Cross-border services Digital Payments and Cross-Border Trade One of the major challenges facing African businesses is the ability to make and receive payments efficiently across borders. Digital payment infrastructure can help address this challenge by making transactions faster, more accessible and potentially less expensive. For an entrepreneur selling products to customers in another African country, for example, a reliable digital payment system can reduce the friction involved in completing a transaction. This is particularly important for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) , which may not have the resources to navigate complicated international payment systems. How ADAPT Can Support African Businesses The success of a continental market ultimately depends on whether businesses can actually use it. Digital infrastructure can help businesses participate in the African market by making it easier to: Discover customers in other countries Receive digital payments Verify customers and business partners Access market information Complete administrative procedures Provide digital services across borders Participate in e-commerce Expand into new African markets This could be particularly valuable for entrepreneurs and MSMEs seeking to expand beyond their domestic markets. Visit HERE to learn more about the AfCFTA and ADAPT: Building a Connected Digital Single Market for Africa ADAPT and Digital Trade Digital trade is becoming increasingly important to Africa s economic future. Businesses no longer need to physically establish an office in another country to serve customers there. A company can sell products through an online platform, provide professional services remotely, receive digital payments and communicate with customers across borders. However, this requires supporting infrastructure. ADAPT can therefore be viewed as part of the digital foundation required for AfCFTA to function effectively in an increasingly digital economy. Who Can Benefit From a More Connected African Market? The benefits of a digitally connected African market could extend across several groups, including: 1. Entrepreneurs and MSMEs Small businesses could gain access to customers and suppliers in markets beyond their home countries. 2. Digital Businesses Technology companies, e-commerce platforms and fintech businesses could benefit from a larger potential market. 3. Consumers Consumers could potentially gain access to a wider variety of African products and services. 4. Governments Governments can benefit from improved digital systems for trade administration, regulation and economic planning. 5. Investors A more integrated African market can create opportunities for investment in businesses, infrastructure and digital services. 6. Professional Service Providers Consultants, software developers, designers, financial professionals and other service providers can potentially serve clients across borders through digital platforms. The Bigger Vision: One African Market AfCFTA s ultimate ambition is not simply to increase the number of products traded between African countries. It is about creating an environment where African businesses can increasingly think of Africa as a market rather than only their individual national economies . Digital infrastructure is an important part of making this possible. A trader in Zambia, for example, should increasingly be able to explore opportunities in another African market, communicate with potential customers, verify business information, complete transactions and receive payment without being overwhelmed by unnecessary administrative and technological barriers. ENQUERIES Conclusion The African Continental Free Trade Area provides the framework for greater economic integration across Africa, while initiatives such as ADAPT focus on the digital infrastructure required to support that integration. Digital identity, data and payments may appear to be separate technologies, but together they form an important foundation for modern cross-border commerce. As Africa continues to expand its digital economy, building interoperable infrastructure will be essential to ensuring that entrepreneurs, MSMEs, consumers and governments can participate in a genuinely connected continental market. title: DAAD Study Scholarships for STEM Disciplines 2027/28: Fully Funded Master’s Opportunity in Germany for Students from Developing and Emerging Countries
summary: The DAAD Study Scholarships for STEM Disciplines offer high-achieving students from developing and emerging countries an opportunity to pursue a full-time Master’s degree in mathematics, computer science, natural sciences or engineering at a university in Germany . The programme is designed to support talented young academics and future professionals who want to build advanced expertise in innovation-driven STEM fields and use that knowledge to strengthen their academic and professional careers. Funding can be provided for 10 to 24 months , depending on the standard duration of the selected Master’s programme, with funding beginning in 2027 . About the DAAD STEM Scholarship The German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) provides scholarships to international students and researchers seeking to study or conduct research in Germany. The Study Scholarships for STEM Disciplines specifically target students from developing and emerging countries who have demonstrated strong academic performance and want to pursue a Master’s degree in one of the following areas: Mathematics Computer Science Natural Sciences Engineering The programme focuses on STEM fields that contribute to innovation, technological development and the future workforce. Successful applicants can study at a state or state-recognised university in Germany , provided that their chosen programme meets the scholarship requirements. What the Scholarship Covers The scholarship provides substantial financial support throughout the funded study period. Successful scholars receive: €992 per month as a scholarship payment. Payments toward health, accident and personal liability insurance . A travel allowance , subject to the applicable conditions and application. An annual study allowance of €460 . Depending on individual circumstances and eligibility, additional support may also be available. Additional Benefits Scholars may be able to apply for: A monthly rent subsidy . A monthly allowance for accompanying family members. Additional financial support related to disability or chronic illness where justified costs are not covered elsewhere. Reimbursement of carbon-offset payments for air travel . Language-learning support. For scholarship periods longer than six months, DAAD may also provide support for language learning, including: Fees for an online language course. A German language course in Germany before the start of the study programme, where DAAD determines that this is necessary. An allowance for a personally selected German language course during the scholarship period. Reimbursement of fees for TestDaF or DSH examinations under the applicable conditions. Important: The Master’s Programme Must Be Tuition-Free One of the most important requirements is that applicants must select a tuition-free Master’s programme . The DAAD scholarship itself does not cover tuition fees . Therefore, applicants should carefully check the tuition arrangements of their chosen university and degree programme before applying. The selected programme must also be: Full-time. On-campus. At a state or state-recognised university in Germany. In mathematics, computer science, natural sciences or engineering. Tuition-free. Starting in the winter semester 2027/28 . Interdisciplinary programmes can qualify if they have a clearly designated STEM focus. Programmes that have already started in Germany cannot receive funding under this scholarship. Programmes that include integrated study periods outside Germany are also excluded. Who Can Apply? The scholarship is aimed at high-achieving students from developing and emerging countries who intend to pursue a STEM Master’s degree in Germany. Applicants must have completed a first university degree recognised in Germany, such as a Bachelor’s degree , by the application deadline at the latest. Applicants who already hold a Master’s degree by the application deadline are not eligible for this particular scholarship programme. The scholarship is therefore particularly relevant to students who have completed their undergraduate studies and are now looking to advance their education through a STEM Master’s programme in Germany. APPLY HERE Eligible Fields of Study Applicants must choose a qualifying programme within the STEM disciplines. 1. Mathematics This can include eligible Master s programmes focused on areas such as mathematics, applied mathematics, statistics and related mathematical disciplines. 2. Computer Science Relevant programmes may include computer science, information technology, software-related disciplines, artificial intelligence and other qualifying computing fields. 3. Natural Sciences This category covers qualifying programmes within the natural sciences. 4. Engineering Applicants may pursue eligible engineering disciplines offered by German universities. For interdisciplinary programmes, applicants should ensure that the programme has a clearly defined STEM focus. Duration of the Scholarship The scholarship can support students for between 10 and 24 months . The actual duration depends on the standard length of the selected Master s degree. For example, if the chosen Master s programme normally takes two years to complete, the applicant should request the scholarship for the full two-year period in the application. After the first year, the scholar s academic performance will be reviewed. If the academic progress indicates that the student is likely to successfully complete the programme within a reasonable period, funding can continue as planned. Funding must begin in 2027 and normally starts on 1 October 2027 , although it may begin earlier if the scholar is required to complete a German language course before starting the degree. Selection Process DAAD states that only applications containing all mandatory documents will be considered. Incomplete applications can be excluded from the selection process for formal reasons. The selection process involves several important stages. 1. Application Review and Pre-Selection Applications are initially assessed based on the submitted documents. Particular attention is given to: Academic achievements. Previous course of study. Language skills. Relevant internships. Relevant professional experience, where applicable. Applicants who perform strongly during the initial assessment may be pre-selected. 2. Interview Pre-selected applicants are invited to an interview with an independent selection committee consisting of university teachers. The interview may take place either physically or virtually. The interview is an important part of the selection process because it allows the committee to assess the applicant s motivation, authenticity, academic plans and personal potential. Key Selection Criteria Applicants are assessed across several major areas. Academic Qualification The committee considers: Academic performance. Previous studies. Knowledge of the language of instruction or working language. Relevant internships and work experience where applicable. Strong academic preparation is therefore an important part of a competitive application. Quality of the Study Project Applicants must demonstrate that they have carefully considered their proposed study programme. The committee considers: The quality of the proposed study project. Preparation for the study programme. Knowledge of the selected degree programme. Choice of university. Evidence of preliminary research. Contacts established with the prospective university where applicable. How the proposed Master s degree fits into the applicant s broader academic and professional development. Applicants should therefore avoid selecting a programme without explaining why it is relevant to their long-term goals. Personal and Professional Potential The committee also considers the applicant s potential and motivation. This includes: Academic motivation. Personal reasons for studying in Germany. German language skills where relevant. Expected academic development. Expected professional development. Personal development. Extracurricular activities. Social commitment. Relevant knowledge and skills. Applicants should demonstrate not only that they are academically capable, but also that the opportunity will contribute meaningfully to their future plans. Equal Opportunity Considerations DAAD also takes equal-opportunity considerations into account during the selection process. Applicants may provide information about special circumstances that may have affected their educational or professional journey. Examples include: Disability. Chronic or prolonged illness. Raising children. Caring for relatives. Refugee background. Significant employment responsibilities required to finance studies. Applicants who have experienced such circumstances can provide relevant information in the application form so that the selection committee can consider their situation appropriately. When Does Funding Begin? The scholarship funding must begin in 2027 . The normal starting date is 1 October 2027 , although an earlier start may be possible when a German language course is required before the Master s programme begins. The scholarship is specifically intended for Master s programmes beginning in the winter term 2027/28 . Application Deadline Deadline: The information provided does not state a single universal application deadline. Applicants should therefore check the official DAAD scholarship database and the specific application information applicable to their country of origin and programme before preparing their submission. Because application deadlines can be tied to the relevant DAAD call and applicant country, prospective applicants should not assume that one deadline applies to everyone. Visit HERE to learn about the DAAD Study Scholarships for STEM Disciplines 2027/28 How to Prepare a Strong Application Applicants should begin preparing well in advance rather than waiting until the application period is close to closing. A strong application should clearly demonstrate: Strong academic performance Highlight relevant academic achievements and STEM-related coursework. A clear study plan Explain why the chosen Master s programme is appropriate for your academic and professional development. A suitable German university Research universities and tuition-free STEM Master s programmes carefully before applying. Strong motivation Clearly explain why studying in Germany is important for your future. Relevant experience Include internships, employment, research, projects and other experiences relevant to your chosen field. Language preparation Pay attention to the language requirements of the selected programme and demonstrate the required language skills. Complete documentation Make sure every mandatory document is submitted because incomplete applications can be excluded from consideration. Why This Opportunity Matters The DAAD STEM scholarship can provide international students with an opportunity to gain advanced academic qualifications in one of Europe s major centres for science, technology and innovation. For students from developing and emerging countries, completing a STEM Master s degree in Germany can provide access to advanced academic environments, international networks and professional development opportunities. The scholarship is particularly valuable because it combines a monthly financial allowance with additional support for insurance, travel and study-related expenses, subject to the programme s conditions. Conclusion The DAAD Study Scholarships for STEM Disciplines provide an important opportunity for talented students from developing and emerging countries to pursue a tuition-free Master s degree in Germany in mathematics, computer science, natural sciences or engineering. With funding of €992 per month , insurance support, a study allowance, travel assistance and potential additional benefits, the programme can significantly reduce the financial burden associated with studying abroad. However, applicants should pay close attention to the eligibility requirements. They must have completed a recognised first degree by the relevant deadline, must not already hold a Master s degree, and must choose an eligible tuition-free STEM Master s programme beginning in the 2027/28 winter term. Prospective applicants should begin researching eligible German universities and programmes early and consult the official DAAD scholarship database for the exact application deadline and country-specific requirements. The Whitley Awards are annual conservation awards that recognise grassroots conservation leaders working to address biodiversity challenges through practical, science-based solutions. The awards are designed to support conservationists who are already implementing projects with demonstrated potential and who need additional funding to expand or strengthen their impact. The Whitley Awards place considerable importance on solutions that are: Rooted in science; Embedded within local communities; Focused on practical conservation action; Designed to deliver lasting impact; Connected to local knowledge and community engagement; and Capable of being scaled up with additional support.
